1.pericope_label: And in that day thou shalt say, O Lord, I will praise thee: though thou wast angry with me, thine anger is turned away, and thou comfortedst me

schools.summary: Gill compares the song to what Israel sang on being brought through the Red sea, that deliverance being typical of salvation by Christ, and takes the day meant to be the Gospel day. Calvin reads the whole as an exhortation with a second purpose, that the promise may be the more fully believed, since a form of thanksgiving is put into their mouth and would not have been given if the grounds were not just and solid; God’s aim in doing good to his church is that the remembrance of his name be extolled, not because he needs our praise but because it profits us, and it is an honour that he condescends to use the services of people altogether useless in themselves. He observes that the whole people is addressed as one man, because it was their duty to be so united, and draws the same requirement for those who wish their prayers and thanksgivings accepted; and he finds the leading thought to be that God, though justly offended, was satisfied with a moderate chastisement and showed himself willing to be pacified. On the disputed particle he reports that some render it because but holds that it can also mean although, citing a scholar who finds the Hebrew construction exactly that of a sentence in one of the epistles, and allows a further rendering from the future tense, that the temporal chastisement will not prevent God from having compassion at length. Whichever is taken, he says, the sentiment matters, since a conviction of God’s anger prompts despair as soon as it seizes the mind and will overwhelm a man unless seasonably counteracted, Satan using every expedient to drive him there.

Henry works on the two words thou shalt say, which mean first that the church will have cause to say it, the promise being sure and its blessings so rich that they furnish abundant matter for thanksgiving, and second that she will have a heart to say it, since God crowns his other gifts with the grace to ascribe all their glory to him. He takes the scattered church, united into one body, to praise God as one man with one mind and one mouth; turns the verse against envy, since when many are brought home to Christ the right response is not to grudge the reception they find, as the Jews grudged the favour shown to the Gentiles, but to give thanks for grace shown to others as well as to ourselves; and presses the concession hardest of all, that even God’s frowns must not put us out of tune for praising him, since he has often just cause to be angry with us while we have never any reason to be angry with him.

Clarke thinks the hymn much better calculated for the Christian church than for the Jewish in any circumstances that can be assigned, and observes that the Jews themselves seem to have applied it to the times of the Messiah, his evidence being the ceremony of the last day of the feast of tabernacles, when water was fetched in a golden pitcher from the fountain of Shiloah at the foot of Mount Sion, carried through the water-gate into the temple and poured with wine on the sacrifice as it lay on the altar; the custom is nowhere ordained in the law of Moses, so he concludes it was taken up as an emblem of future blessings in allusion to the third verse of this chapter, and reports that our Saviour applied the ceremony to himself and to the effusion of the Holy Spirit. He supports the reading from the Talmud, which asks why the place was called the house of drawing and answers that from thence they drew the Holy Spirit, from a Jewish commentator who makes the water divine knowledge and the wells the teachers of righteousness, and from the Targum, which has receiving with joy a new doctrine from the chosen among the righteous, which Clarke takes for the Gospel. On the disputed particle he identifies the Hebrew idiom with a sentence of the apostle and complains that the Septuagint and Vulgate kept too close to it. Wesley dates the day by the event, when the recovery of Israel and the conversion of the Gentiles is fulfilled.

Ellicott makes the prophet the psalmist of a new Exodus, the hymn built on the type of the older song though with less local and historical colouring, and finds in its opening that confession must be blended with thanksgiving, since only those who have first felt God’s wrath can rightly estimate the comfort he gives. That a prophet should appear as a psalmist he takes as a natural result of the training of the schools of the prophets, and possibly of familiarity with the Temple service as a priest or Levite, noting that the psalms ascribed to the sons of Korah present so many parallelisms to this writer and belong so obviously to the same period that he may reasonably be thought to have been associated with that company.

debates: Does the particle mean because or although? Calvin reports both, prefers although, and cites a scholar who matches the Hebrew construction to a sentence in one of the epistles; Clarke makes the same identification and faults the Septuagint and Vulgate for keeping too close to the idiom.

For whom was the hymn written? Clarke holds it much better suited to the Christian church than to the Jewish in any circumstances, while noting that the Jews themselves applied it to the times of the Messiah; Henry gives it to both, the Jewish church at its deliverances and the Christian at the setting up of the kingdom; Ellicott makes it the song of a new Exodus.

How should praise and anger stand together? Ellicott makes confession the condition of rightly valuing comfort; Henry insists that God’s frowns must not put us out of tune; Calvin warns that a conviction of anger left uncounteracted ends in despair.
outliers: Clarke describes the water-drawing of the feast of tabernacles, from the fountain of Shiloah through the water-gate to the altar, and traces the custom to this chapter rather than to the law of Moses.
Ellicott suggests the prophet may have been associated with the sons of Korah, whose psalms run close to his language and belong to the same period.
Clarke reports the Targum rendering of the third verse as receiving with joy a new doctrine from the chosen among the righteous, and asks whether the paraphrast spoke as a prophet.
themes: a song for the Gospel day

2.pericope_label: Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid: for the Lord Jehovah is my strength and my song; he also is become my salvation. Therefore with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation

schools.summary: Gill takes the opening word to do four things at once, asserting the fact, expressing wonder at it, excluding every other saviour, and directing others to the only one to look to; and he identifies the salvation with Christ, who as God is fit to be a Saviour and has become the author of a salvation no creature could be. On the drawing of water he allows the words to be an exhortation to others, as two versions render them, an encouragement by the church’s own example, or a prophecy that they shall do it; the water is grace, so called because it softens, purifies, cools and refreshes and extinguishes thirst, the well is deep and not within everyone’s reach, the bucket is faith and is itself the gift of God, and the drawing is done in the use of means, by prayer, reading and attendance on the word and ordinances, where faith draws hard and receives much. Calvin makes the same opening word the hinge but as evidence of a change in the kind of knowledge involved, since it is right to behold God’s salvation by faith in the midst of afflictions but here the prophet speaks of knowledge derived from experience, a countenance hidden for a time now shining out so that it may be pointed at with the finger; he draws from it the order that confidence proceeds from faith as an effect from its cause, so that where faith is wanting there can be no peace of conscience. On the third verse he makes the salvation of God a constantly running fountain set before them, and since nothing in life is more necessary than water, takes the part for the whole, so that everything needed to support life flows from God’s undeserved goodness; his mercy satisfies the thirsty, refreshes the parched and revives the worn out, and we ought to be like dry ground desiring the waters of the Lord, since God does not leave us burning with unsatisfied desire but sets fountains before us, and that is Christ, of whose fulness all have received.

Clarke suspects that the shorter of the two divine names is a copyist’s error, and explains how it could arise, since a scribe who found a line too short would fill it with as many letters as it would hold and then begin the next line with the whole word, so that the first two letters might stand at the end of one line and the full name at the head of the next; he supports the suspicion from manuscripts and from the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac and Arabic, which omit the shorter name, notes that the pronoun in my song is necessary and is supplied by three of those versions, and reports further copies that omit the longer name or run the two together. Wesley says of the second verse only that the salvation was brought to pass not by man but by the almighty power of God, and of the third that thirsty souls are filled with divine graces and comforts drawn from God in the use of gospel ordinances.

Ellicott allows the opening to be rendered either God is my salvation or the God of my salvation, and insists that on either construction salvation means more than deliverance from danger and includes the highest spiritual blessings; he marks the exceptional combination of the two divine names, which occurs in only one other place, and notes that apart from it the second clause is a verbal reproduction of the older song. On the drawing of water he renders the opening word literally as and, allows the clause to be either part of the hymn or an address to those who are to join in it and prefers the latter as more in harmony with the context, and describes the later ritual of the Feast of Tabernacles, in which the priests went in solemn procession to the Pool of Siloam, filled a golden vase, carried it to the Temple and poured it out on the western side of the altar of burnt offering while the people chanted the great Hallel; if that represented the ritual of the monarchy, he infers, the prophet’s words pointed to it, and he adds that the Talmud expressly connects the act with this symbolism and that the same prophet’s earlier reference to the waters of Shiloah confirms the inference. Keil and Delitzsch hear in the third verse a prophetic promise pointing back to the opening of the chapter, and set it against the wilderness, since as Israel was miraculously supplied with water in the desert, so the God who has become their salvation will open many and manifold sources of salvation from which they may draw at their heart’s delight.

debates: Is the shorter divine name original? Clarke takes it for a copyist’s error and explains the scribal habit that would produce it, citing manuscripts and four old versions that lack it; Ellicott keeps the doubled name and treats it as an exceptional but genuine combination found in one other place.

Are the words about drawing water part of the hymn or addressed to those who sing it? Ellicott prefers the address as more in harmony with the context; Gill allows exhortation, example or prophecy; Keil and Delitzsch take the verse as a promise pointing back to the chapter’s opening.

What is the water? Gill makes it grace, drawn by faith in the use of means; Calvin makes it the whole of what supports life, flowing from undeserved goodness, and finally Christ; Ellicott and the Talmud he cites connect it with the water-drawing of the Feast of Tabernacles.
outliers: Clarke explains the doubled divine name from a scribe’s habit of filling out a short line with the first letters of a word and then writing the whole word at the head of the next.
Ellicott describes the procession to the Pool of Siloam, the golden vase, and the water poured beside the altar while the people chanted the great Hallel.
Keil and Delitzsch compare the wells of salvation with the water miraculously supplied to Israel in the desert.
themes: two divine names in one clause

4.pericope_label: And in that day shall ye say, Praise the Lord, call upon his name, declare his doings among the people, make mention that his name is exalted. Sing unto the Lord; for he hath done excellent things: this is known in all the earth. Cry out and shout, thou inhabitant of Zion: for great is the Holy One of Israel in the midst of thee

schools.summary: Calvin takes the same turn outward and presses it two ways, that they should speak not to one but to all, and not at one time only but throughout their whole life; he uses the phrase about calling on the name to define worship, since it is enjoined that we may not glory in anything else and Scripture frequently puts that one act for the whole, by which we show where our confidence is placed. The deliverance he thinks too excellent to be proclaimed in a corner, so that it must go through the whole world, first to the Jews and afterwards to all, which makes the exhortation a forerunner of the preaching of the gospel. He warns that those who exhort others must not sit down in indolence themselves, nothing being more absurd than lazy men stirring up others to praise God, and insists there is abundant ground for the singing, since God holds out a rich subject of it in the work of reconciling us to himself and destroying the dominion of death; that the thing is known in all the earth he takes as a glance at the calling of the Gentiles. On the closing title he makes it do two things, the Holy One so that reverence may not be mere terror but the mark of a peculiar care, and of Israel from the effect, since by gathering and saving a people God may be said to have become their own property; our whole happiness is to have God dwelling with us, without which a life full of riches would still be wretched, his presence filling us with inconceivable joy and his absence leaving us exposed to grief. Gill keeps the singing concrete, psalms and hymns and spiritual songs sung vocally and together as churches do, while allowing a second construction by which the Lord himself is the subject matter of the song; he takes the praise to be especially proper to Gospel times and more so in the latter day, when the kingdom of Christ will be enlarged and the church glorious, her walls salvation and her gates praise.

Henry calls this the second part of the song and marks the change of direction, since in the first part believers stir up themselves while here they invite and encourage one another and contrive to spread the praise further. He identifies those addressed as the inhabitants of Zion and Jerusalem, whom God had particularly protected, and holds that those who have received distinguishing favours ought to be the most forward in praising; he notes that the word for the inhabitant is feminine and turns it into an exhortation, that the weaker sex be strong in the Lord and out of their mouth praise be perfected. On the manner of praising he gives two heads, prayer, since giving thanks for former mercy is a decent way of begging further mercy and begging further mercy is itself accepted as a thankful acknowledgment of what has been received, and preaching and writing, since we must not only speak to God but speak to others concerning him, and not only call upon his name but proclaim it.

Clarke reads the call upon the name as a commission to preach him who is the Root of Jesse and stands as an ensign for the nations, and to call the people to believe in him, since in him alone salvation is to be found. On the last verse he widens the address beyond the Jewish people, to whom the word of salvation was to be sent first, so as to take in all members of the church of Christ, since the Holy One of Israel dwells in them, and supports it from the apostle’s summary of the mystery proclaimed among the Gentiles, Christ in you, the hope of glory.

Ellicott renders the phrase literally as among the peoples and notes that the prophet is quoting the hymn sung when the Ark was placed in Zion, and in part a psalm; he hears in the reason given for singing another echo of the older song, where God is said to have triumphed gloriously. On the last verse he observes that the Hebrew is feminine, so that the inhabitant is the daughter of Zion, the restored Church that has Zion for her dwelling-place, and that the hymn ends with the divine name characteristic of this prophet, whose presence was to be a joy and blessing to the remnant worthy of their calling; with this hymn, he adds, the whole of what has been called the Immanuel volume of the prophecies comes to its close. Keil and Delitzsch print these verses without comment.

debates: Who is called on to praise? Henry names the inhabitants of Zion and Jerusalem who had been protected, and makes the feminine form an exhortation to the weaker sex; Clarke widens the address past the Jewish people to all members of the church; Ellicott takes the inhabitant as the daughter of Zion, the restored church.

How far should the praise reach? Calvin holds the deliverance too excellent to be proclaimed in a corner and makes the exhortation a forerunner of gospel preaching; Clarke turns the clause into a commission to preach the Root of Jesse to the nations; Ellicott traces the words themselves back to an older hymn.

What does the closing title carry? Calvin makes the Holy One guard reverence from mere terror and of Israel record the effect of gathering a people; Ellicott makes it the name characteristic of this prophet and the seal of the volume it closes.
outliers: Henry observes that giving thanks for former mercy is a decent way of begging further mercy, and that begging further mercy is accepted as a thankful acknowledgment.
Calvin remarks that nothing is more absurd than lazy men stirring up others to praise God.
Ellicott notes that this hymn closes what has been called the Immanuel volume of the prophecies.
themes: calling on the name as the whole of worship
a deliverance too great for a corner
a volume brought to its close
